description: Internet has now become a crucial element of daily life, aiding people with conveniences in purchasing, money transaction and communication. However, there has been a rise in online fraud cases in India. Victims are frequently targeted through various forms of cybercrimes including phishing, identity theft and fake online transactions, which cause significant monetary loss and emotional suffering. The current research will evaluate the effectiveness of Indian legislation in tackling online fraud. This paper will analyze essential legislation including the Information Technology Act of 2000 along with other relevant legislation and guidelines. The analysis will be done based on information gathered from scholarly journals, official documents, and online sources. The results show that while there is enough legislation in place to counter the problem of online fraud in India, their efficiency is hindered by issues like lack of awareness among the public and long legal procedures involved. The conclusion states that while India has made substantial progress in combating the issue of online fraud, more needs to be done in order to increase system effectiveness.

Online Fraud and Legal Protection under

A Critical Analysis of Legal Remedies and 
Their Effectiveness in India 
 
1Husna Kounain, 2 Hunain Fathima, 3Huma, 4Mayuri, 5M.

ABSTRACT 
Internet has now become a crucial element of daily life, 
aiding people with conveniences in purchasing, money 
transaction and communication. However, there has been 
a rise in online fraud cases in India. Victims are frequently 
targeted through various forms of cybercrimes including 
phishing, identity theft and fake onl ine transactions, which 
cause significant monetary  loss and emotional suffering. 
The current research will evaluate the  effectiveness of 
Indian legislation in tackling online fraud. This paper will 
analyze essential legislation including the Information 
Technology Act of 2000 along with other relevant 
legislation and guidelines. The analysis will be done based 
on information gathered from scholarly journals, official 
documents, and online sources. The results show that while 
there is enough legislation in place to counter the problem 
of online fraud in India, their efficiency is  hindered by 
issues like lack of awareness among the public and long 
legal procedures involved. The conclusion states that while 
India has made substantial progress in combating the  issue 
of online fraud, more needs to be done in order to increase 
system effectiveness. 
 
Keywords: fraud, cybercrime, Information Technology  Act 
2000 legal remedies, phishing, digital payments.

1. INTRODUCTION 
Internet access has become an 
indispensable necessity of modern-day life 
in India. People  pay for services u sing 
their mobile phones; perform bank 
transactions using UPI (Unified Payment 
Interface); engage in online shopping; and 
handle various financial matters without 
even visiting the banks. Currently, there 
are more than 931 million internet users in 
India, with UPI  carrying out billions of  
transactions annually, indicating a  quick 
development of the "Digital India." 
However, there are always risks associated 
with every new technological 
advancement because every internet user 
becomes a victim of cybercrimina ls' 
activities. 
Online fraud, which can be described as a 
deception committed on the digital 
platform with a purpose of appropriating 
money from people, is one of the 
significant problems faced by  India 
recently. Over the past few years, 
millions of complaints about various 
types of cybercrimes were filed against 
fraudsters who applied such methods as 
phishing, fake KYC updates, lottery 
scams, and impersonation, causing huge 
financial damages to their victims. At the 
same time, many ordinary people who are 
not technologically literate find the usage 
of the internet a risky business.The 
government of India has undertaken 
several legal steps to address the problem. 
There are certain legislative acts and 
guidelines that can help tackle the issue at 
hand, such as the Information Technology 
Act 2000, sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya 
Sanhita, and guidelines set forth by RBI. 
There are also special mechanisms like 
cyber crime portals and helplines, as well 
as cyber cells designed to aid the victims 
of such crimes. 
Nevertheless, the current legal approaches 
do not seem to work effectively enough. 
Even though there are lots of cases of 
online fraud reported annually, the number 
of convictions does not seem to grow 
accordingly, and the majority of the 
victims find it hard to recover their losses. 
Some of the reasons behind that may be 
associated with inadequate enforcement of 
the legislation and delayed investigation 
procedures, thus resulting in the 
mentioned gaps. Accordingly, the research 
question of this paper i s as follows: "Are 
legal remedies for online fraud in India 
sufficient?" 
Study Objectives 
 
 To determine whether legal 
solutions for online fraud cases in India 
are adequate. 
 To study  the Laws relating  to 
online fraud. 
 To assess the efficacy of the legal 
solutions available. 
 To highlight difficulties 
encountered in implementation. 
 To propose solutions for 
improvement. 
 
2. LITERATURE REVIEW 
Online fraud is a big problem in India. It is 
happening because more and more people 
are using the internet. There are types of 
online fraud like fake emails, fake identity 
and fake online transactions. The laws in 
India to stop online fraud are good. They 
are not working well. The Information 
Technology Act 2000 is one of the laws to 
stop online fraud. It says that if som eone 
cheats you on the internet they  can be 
punished.. The law is not working well 
because it is not being enforced properly. 
The Reserve Bank of India is also trying 
to stop fraud. They have made some rules 
to help people who have been cheated.. 
Even with  these rules many people are 
still losing their money. The problem is 
that the laws are not being enforced 
properly and the legal process is too slow. 
So we need to make the laws better and 
enforce them properly. 
 
3. RESEARCH METHODOLOGY 
This research follows  an qualitative

approach.Doctrinal research means we 
study and analyse existing laws, court 
judgments and legal rules.We do not 
collect data from surveys or 
experiments.This type of research is 
commonly used in studies.It helps us 
understand what the law says and how it is 
applied in situations. 
3.1 Sources of Data 
This paper uses secondary sources of 
data.Secondary sources are materials 
created by others.Examples include books, 
reports and official documents.The 
sources used in this study are: 
 
 laws and acts: The Information 
Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya 
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
 Government reports: The NCRB 
Crime in India Report 2023 and reports 
from the Indian Cyber Crime 
Coordination Centre (I4C).
 RBI guidelines on banking and 
customer protection.
 books and journal articles on cyber 
law and online fraud.
 News. Case studies related  to 
online fraud incidents in India.
 
3.2 Method of Analysis 
 
The data collected was carefully. 
Analysed.We identified legal provisions 
and checked them against real -world 
situations.Examples include reported fraud 
cases.The effectiveness of  each law  was 
judged based on factors like conviction 
rates.We also looked  at victim recovery  
rates and feedback from reports.This 
helped us understand where the legal 
system is working w ell and where it is 
falling short. 
 
3.3. Scope and Limitations of the Study 
This study is limited to the framework in 
India only.It does not compare laws with 
laws from other countries.The study relies 
entirely on published and publicly 
available documents .We did not collect 
data like interviews or survey’s.The 
findings are based on what has been 
reported and documented.The legal 
framework and online fraud in India are 
the focus of this study.The laws and 
regulations in India are crucial in 
understanding fr aud.The study on  online 
fraud, in India helps in understanding the 
system in India. 
 
4. LEGAL FRAMEWORK 
India has a lot of laws and rules that deal 
with fraud. This section will explain the 
important ones in a simple way. 
 
4.1 The Information Technology Act, 
2000 (IT Act) 
The Information Technology Act, 2000 is 
the law in India that deals with 
cybercrime. The Indian Parliament passed 
the Information Technology Act, 2000 to 
control the use of computers and the 
internet. Some of its sections that relate to 
online fraud are: 
 
 Section 43: If someone uses 
another person’s computer without 
permission and causes damage they have 
to pay compensation to the person who 
owns the computer.
 Section 66: If someone does 
something or commits fraud using a 
computer they can be puni shed with up to 
3 years in prison or a fine of up to Rs. 5 
Lakh or both.
 Section 66C: This section punishes 
people who steal someone’s identity like 
their password or Aadhaar number 
without their permission. The punishment 
is up to 3 years in prison and a fine of up 
to Rs. 1 Lakh.
 Section 66D: This section 
punishes people who cheat by 
impersonating someone using a computer 
or communication device. The punishment 
is up to 3 years in prison and a fine of up 
to Rs. 1 Lakh.
4.2 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,  2023 
(BNS)

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 
replaced the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The 
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 includes 
rules to deal with modern crimes, 
including online fraud. Key sections 
include: 
 Section 318: This section deals 
with cheating and dishonesty.  If someone 
cheats another person, including through 
means they can be punished with up to 3 
years in prison.
 Section 319: This section deals 
with cheating by impersonation, which 
means pretending to be someone to cheat. 
This is directly relevant to arrest  scams 
and phishing.
 Section 111: This section deals 
with crime, which can be applied when a 
group of people run a large online fraud 
operation together.
 
4.3 Reserve Bank of India  (RBI) 
Guidelines 
The Reserve Bank of India has issued 
guidelines to protect cus tomers from 
losses due to online fraud. According to 
the Reserve Bank of India circular of 2017 
on limiting customer liability in banking 
transactions: 
 
 If the banks own system is at fault 
the customer is not responsible for any 
loss.
 If a third party is responsible not 
the bank and not the customer the 
customers maximum liability depends on 
how they report the fraud.
 If the customer reports the fraud 
within 3 working days they are not 
liable for any loss.
 
These guidelines are meant to ensure that 
customers are protected and that banks 
take responsibility for the security of 
transactions. 
 
4.4 Cybercrime Reporting System: 
Helpline 1930 
The Government of India through the 
Ministry of Home Affairs has set up a 
National Cybercrime Helpline number 
1930 and a portal, at 
www.cybercrime.gov.in. These are meant 
to help victims report cybercrime quickly. 
The system can also help freeze money in 
accounts if the online fraud is reported in 
time. This is called the Citizen Financial 
Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management 
System (CFCFRMS) of the Government 
of India. 
 
5. ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION 
India has taken steps to fight online fraud 
by setting up helplines and reporting 
systems like the  cybercrime helpline that 
you can call at 1930. These systems help 
stop some losses by acting such as 
freezing suspicious accounts. However 
they only work well if peopl e report  the 
crime away and the police respond 
quickly. 
The big problem is that cybercriminals are 
much faster than the law. They can do 
transactions in just a few minutes and use 
many accounts in different places. On the 
hand it takes a long time to report a crime 
and investigate it. This delay gives the 
guys time to move or withdraw the money 
before anything can be done.Another issue 
is that important institutions like  banks, 
police and regulatory bodies do not work 
together. People who are victims o ften get 
confused because they are sent from one 
authority to another, which makes the 
process even slower. Although there are 
systems that bring everything together 
they do not work smoothly which makes it 
hard to handle cases.If we look at the 
numbers we  can see that the current 
system has some flaws. Cybercrime cases 
are going up every year. Not many people 
are convicted.. To make things worse only  
a small amount of the stolen money is ever 
recovered. This shows that the laws we 
have are not working well . They  are not 
stopping cybercriminals and they are not 
giving victims the justice they deserve. 
 
 
Recent Trends in Cyber Criminology Research 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Page No. 43    http://www.hbrppublication.com                                                 2026:  2 (2), 39 -46 
The nature of cybercrime makes it hard to 
enforce the law. Digital evidence can be 
hard to find and keep and many cases 
involve places, including other countri es. 
These things create procedural challenges 
slowing down investigations and making 
it harder to prosecute the bad guys 
effectively.Victims also have a  time 
getting their money back. Even when fake  
accounts are found and money is frozen 
the process of get ting the money often 
involves long legal procedures extra costs 
and going to court. This discourages 
people from seeking justice and reduces 
the value of the help that is available. 
Overall while India has a framework with 
laws like the Information Technology Act, 
2000 it does not work well in practice. 
Issues like delays, poor coordination, low 
conviction rates, lack of awareness and 
not enough accountability from 
institutions reduce the impact of the laws. 
Therefore it can be said that the system 
only wor ks a little and needs 
improvements in how it is implemented 
enforced and made known to the public to 
provide adequate protection. 
5.1 Case Study: Online Fraud and 
Legal Remedies in Practice 
 
There is a type of fraud in India called the 
"digital arrest" scam. I t is when someone 
pretends to be a police officer and cheats 
you. In 2025 an old man in Delhi was 
cheated by someone who pretended to be 
a police officer. The man was told that he 
had done something and he had to pay a 
fine. He was cheated of ₹5 lakh. 
When it comes to the law the authorities 
took action using the Information 
Technology Act from 2000 Section 66D, 
which deals with cheating by pretending 
to be someone else. They also used rules 
from the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita to 
tackle organized crime. Accord ing to 
reports the authorities were able to freeze 
some of the stolen money using the 
cybercrime helpline and related systems. 
However they could not recover a lot of 
the money because it was transferred 
quickly and hidden in channels like 
multiple accounts and digital assets. 
 
5.2 COMMON TYPES OF ONLINE 
FRAUD IN INDIA : 
5.2.1. OTP Fraud: The Stolen Key 
OTP fraud is a game where a criminal 
tricks you into giving them the key" to 
your bank account. Scammers usually 
pretend to be bank officials or delivery 
agents to create panic. Once you give 
them the secret code they can instantly 
take your money. 
 
5.2.2 Online Shopping Fraud: The Fake 
Deal 
Online shopping fraud is when someone 
cheats you by pretending to sell you 
something. They take your money. You do 
not get what you paid for. 
5.2.3. Digital Payment Fraud: The 
Reverse Trap 
You should be careful with some apps like 
the ones that use UPI. There is a scam 
going around that uses "Collect Requests”. 
It looks like you are getting cash back or a 
refund. Really it is a trick. Th e scammer 
tries to get you to enter your PIN and 
when you do it does not give you money it 
actually sends money to them. 
5.2.4. Victim Blaming: The Invisible 
Barrier 
When something goes wrong like money 
getting stolen banks and police sometimes 
say it is the pers ons fault because they did 
something wrong. This means the banks 
and police do not have to give the person 
their money or do anything to help. 
 
6. FINDINGS 
Based on the analysis of existing laws 
official reports and case studies here are 
the key findings of this study: 
 Rising Cybercrime Numbers: 
According to NCRB (2024) cybercrime 
complaints in India have increased every 
year. Cybercrime is on the rise in India 
and online fraud is becoming more

Page No. 44    http://www.hbrppublication.com                                                 2026:  2 (2), 39 -46 
common. 
 Low Conviction Rate: Many cases 
are registered, but the number of people 
convicted and punished for cybercrime is 
very small. This shows that the legal 
process against cybercrime is not 
effective. 
 Poor Money Recovery: In online 
fraud cases victims cannot recover their 
stolen money. Money is quickly 
transferred across accounts and the legal 
process to freeze and return it is too slow. 
Online fraud victims face difficulties in 
recovering their money. 
 Lack of Public Awareness: Many  
people in India in smaller towns and 
villages do not know about cybercrime 
laws the helpline number 1930 or the 
cybercrime portal. This means many 
cybercrimes, including online fraud go 
unreported. 
 Weak Coordination Between 
Agencies: Banks, police and regulatory 
bodies like RBI do  not always 
communicate effectively. This creates  
delays and confusion  in handling fraud 
cases and cybercrime. 
 Digital Arrest Scam is Growing: 
The " arrest" scam is a new and harmful 
type of cybercrime.  It targets less tech-
savvy people causing financial loss and 
mental trauma. Cybercrime, such as arrest 
scams affects many people. 
 Legal Framework Exists but 
Implementation is Weak: India has laws, 
like the IT Act 2000 and the BNS 2023 
that cover cybercrime and online fraud. 
However these laws are not always 
enforced properly. Police often lack the 
technical knowle dge to handle digital 
evidence related to cybercrime. 
  
7. CHALLENGES /LIMITATIONS 
7.1 Challenges in Fighting Online 
Fraud 
 The speed of cybercrime is much 
faster than the speed of law. Criminals can 
move money quickly. It takes time to 
report, investigate and freeze accounts. By 
then the money is usually gone. 
 The -border nature of crime makes 
it hard to catch fraudsters. Many operate 
from countries like Cambodia and 
Myanmar. It is difficult for Indian police 
to take action against people who're not in 
India. O nline fraudsters often hide in 
countries. 
 Digital evidence is tricky to 
handle. It requires technical knowledge 
and tools. Many police stations in smaller 
cities do not have the equipment or 
training. They struggle  to collect and 
preserve evidence. 
 Many vi ctims do not know to 
report fraud. They should call the helpline 
1930 within  3 days to have a chance of 
getting their money back. If they delay it 
reduces the chance of recovery. Online 
fraud victims must report fast. 
 Victims often feel embarrassed. 
Do not  report the crime. This means the 
actual number of frauds is much higher 
than what's officially recorded. Victims of 
online fraud feel ashamed. 
 Some banks do not follow RBI 
guidelines properly. They refuse to 
compensate victims even when they are 
entitled to it. Banks should protect their 
customers. 
7.2 Limitations of This Study 
 
 This study uses existing reports. 
No direct surveys or interviews were 
done, which means the findings depend 
on published reports. The study relies on 
data. 
 This study is  about India and 
does not compare the Indian legal 
system, with other countries. It focuses on 
India’s online fraud problem. 
 Some case studies are based on 
news reports, which may not give the 
picture of the  case. News reports have 
limitations.

Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Responsibility: Reconstructing
Mens Rea and Attribution for AI-Assisted Cybercrime in Pakistan
Author:
Syed Mudassir Shah
Abstract
Artificial intelligence is changing the scale, speed, personalization, and technical complexity of cybercrime without eliminating the need to attribute criminal responsibility to human actors. In Pakistan, the principal substantive framework remains the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016, as amended in 2025, supplemented by the Pakistan Penal Code, the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order 1984, the Electronic Transactions Ordinance 2002, and the National Forensics Agency Act 2024. These laws are largely technology-neutral, yet AI-assisted offending creates evidential and conceptual pressure on traditional categories of intention, knowledge, authorization, causation, participation, and digital attribution. A person may use a generative model to draft phishing messages, automate reconnaissance, generate malicious code, create deepfakes, or optimize fraud while delegating numerous operational choices to software. The central legal problem is therefore not whether an AI system itself possesses criminal mens rea, but how courts should infer the mental state and causal contribution of programmers, operators, deployers, account holders, collaborators, and beneficiaries when machine output intervenes between human instruction and prohibited result. This paper argues against premature recognition of AI as a criminal subject. Current systems lack the normative agency, legal status, and punishment-sensitive interests that make criminal blame meaningful. Pakistani law should instead adopt a human-centred attribution framework built around purposeful use, knowledge of capabilities, control over deployment, foreseeability of system behaviour, acceptance of risk, contribution to the offence, and corroborated digital evidence. The paper proposes a four-layer attribution model covering identity, control, mental state, and causal contribution, together with evidential safeguards for logs, prompts, model outputs, account records, device forensics, and chain of custody. Reform should clarify AI-assisted liability without creating strict criminal responsibility for developers or users merely because an unpredictable model produced harmful output.
